Particularly important was the route from Cracow to Hungary via Bochnia and Sącz, which was older than the foundation of the town. This route led further down the Poprad valley controlled by the castle in Rytro, which was associated with Wenceslaus II of Bohemia38; another variant was the road through the Magurska Pass. The route to Ruthenia and Hungary led from Nowy Sącz through Biecz. The route from Nowy Sącz to Sandomierz – and further on to Ruthenia – was closed in 1329, as its operation infringed on the interests of the Cracow merchants. As in many towns of Lesser Poland, suburbs developed also in Nowy Sącz, with churches founded on their territory. Written sources do not specify the exact location of the hospital with the Church of the Holy Spirit51, the foundation of burgher Mikołaj Kieslink on the basis of a privilege granted by Casimir the Great in 1360, i.e. in the period of foundation of similar complexes in the suburbs of Kazimierz, Wieliczka, Bochnia. The hospital and church probably functioned in Przedmieście Mniejsze (Suburb Minor, Behind the Stone House), where the royal properties were situated. At the turn of the 14th and 15th centuries, thanks to Zydel Lang, a townsman from Sącz, the complex was moved into the town limits (the foundation was approved in 1400 by the Bishop of Cracow, Piotr Wysz52), where it occupied the area of residential plots. In 1409, the church and hospital were handed over to the Norbertines53; their endowment consisted of the above-mentioned villages established on one hundred lans, which Jan Bogacz received in 1299. This complex also replaced the residential plots. The church, destroyed by fires, was rebuilt in 1492 as a brick one-nave church with a three-sided closure on the eastern side. It has partially survived to the present day. In the 15th and 16th centuries, there were also goldsmiths, painters, woodcarvers, carpenters and bricklayers working in Nowy Sącz. development of the town in the modern period: the 16th – mid-17th century In the 16th century, Nowy Sącz reached the apogee of its development, which was reflected in architectural transformations: the fortifications were modernised, the Renaissance town hall and tenement houses were erected. From the turn of the 16th and 17th centuries, signs of decline started to be visible: construction activity targeted mainly the castle and church complexes (but also the stone houses at the market square), whereas the bishop’s mansion was falling into ruin, and further works on the decaying fortifications were basically limited to repairs. The conflict between Poland and Turkey over Wallachia in 1552–1560 triggered the modernisation of the defence system. In 1555, Sigismund Augustus ordered the town to use the income from the bullion warehouse for this purpose. As a result, between 1555 and 1557, a key defensive structure – probably a bastile – was erected on the south side, in front of Węgierska (Hungarian) Gate; its design was prepared by town scribe Szymon Kozielski and the works were managed by mason Albert of Libusza66. The years 1562–1563 brought a complete transformation of the town hall during its reconstruction after the fire. The town hall was recorded as existing on the market square in 152367. It was probably designed by an Italian mason named Lodovico. Exposed foundations, written sources68 and iconography allow us to imagine it as a two-storey building topped with an attic, with a low clock tower with a gallery for the trumpeter and external stairs69. The structure was similar to the one observed in the town halls of Tarnów, Sandomierz and Kazimierz near Cracow. From the middle of the 16th century until the turn of the 16th and 17th centuries, the influence of the Reformation, especially of the Arians, was exceptionally strong in the Sącz region83. At that time the number of inhabitants of Nowy Sącz – including the suburbs – reached 3.5–4 thousand, of which about 1.5 thousand lived in the town centre. The vast majority of the population was already Polish; sermons in German were probably discontinued by the 1560s85. As a result of the Swedish Deluge of 1655–1657 and the Great Northern War of the early 18th century86, the phenomenon of “voids”, characteristic of Polish cities at the time, was growing rapidly: properties in the centre and suburbs were abandoned and not developed by the impoverished burghers. After the invasion of 1659, out of 224 properties recorded in the censuses, as many as 85 were empty, and in the following years this number increased87. The problem was to some extent mitigated by the Jewish settlement, supported by the Lubomirski family (the starosts of Nowy Sącz), which developed in the most ruined part of the town, between the northern block at the market square – the street running there (a section of today’s Franciszkańska Street) was called Mała Żydowska (Little Jewish Street) – and the starost’s castle. The post-partition period paradoxically brought an overcoming of the town’s regression105. Among the investments of that period, we should mention the regulated road and street network, the completion and filling in of the urban space with new brick buildings, the liquidation of monastery complexes, the establishment of colonies for German-speaking settlers, and finally the erection of the modern defensive system. The urban transformation of the town centre was essentially based on the spatial layout of the chartered town; its geometrical arrangement corresponded to the rationalist urban planning principles of the time. Castle of Nowy Sącz was confiscated by the Austrian army to serve as barracks for the local garrison and as a military bakery. The dismantling of a large part of the medieval town walls followed the opinion of the town engineer in 1786 about their poor technical condition. Demolition work was completed in 1804106. In the area of the southern section of the fortifications today’s Wałowa and Szwedzka Streets developed; already in 1771, a “Swedish” chapel was erected there, connected with a local legend about Swedish soldiers buried in this place107. The already mentioned first military topographic map of Galicia (Mieg’s map, 1779–1783) records the field fortifications that surrounded the town centre108. In Hungarian Suburb by the road to Stary Sącz a military hospital for the Nowy Sącz garrison was located at today’s 63 Jagiellońska Street, with the second floor built in 1927/1928, after adaptation for the King Bolesław Chrobry Second State Grammar School)110. The second-order ring road from Tarnów to Hungary, completed probably in the 1880s, after Mieg’s map was drawn up, strongly influenced the development of the town and its suburbs111. The sections of this road drawn in a straight line – in accordance with rationalistic planning principles – are today’s Tarnowska Street (on the northern side) and the section of Jagiellońska Street and św. Kunegunda Street (on the southern side). The initial section of Jagiellońska Street (then Drzewna Street) was incorporated into the original urban layout, corresponding to the course of the street leading south from the southeastern corner of the market square. The reference to the original arrangement consisted in the elimination of a street running out of the middle of the southern frontage of the market square, re-established within the “voids” and recorded on Mieg’s map. The new route attracted buildings: apart from the military hospital there was an inn named Bernaszówka (82 Jagiellońska Street) and suburban mansions, built among others for Austrian officials. Probably at about the same time, a road parallel to the aforementioned section of today’s Jagiellońska Street, i.e. the present Jana Długosza Street, was laid out, also as a straight line. Kazimierza Wielkiego (former Żydowska), ks. Piotra Skargi (Szpitalna) and Dunajewskiego (Furmańska) Streets were widened and straightened. The entrance to the town from the west was regulated: a road was laid out along a straight line which today is Krakowska Street and (roughly) Wodna Street, which involved the construction of a bridge over the Dunajec. Probably around 1830, as part of the “Carpathian” route, an entrance to the town was built from the east, with a bridge over the Kamienica – this was the road to Załubińcze, today’s Lwowska Street. This route concentrated dispersed buildings in the suburb, which was called Piekło (Hell) because of the popular name of a local inn (this name was registered on a cadastral map from 1846). (table 1.1).

A characteristic effect of the settlement patent issued by Emperor Joseph II in 1781 were colonies established mainly for German-speaking settlers throughout the Austrian partition 110 R. Gessing, Zarys dziejów II Państwowego Gimnazjum im. Bolesława 111 K. Dziwik,Rozwój przestrzenny miasta Nowego Sacza od XIII do XIX wieku na tle stosunków gospodarczych, RS, vol. 5, 1962, p. 211. The section between Nowy Sącz and Stary Sącz was in operation in 1703, when the buildings of Kamieniec on the Poprad River were built, cf. Z. Beiers dorf, B. Krasnowolski, Stary Sącz, zarys historii rozwoju prze­ strzennego, Kraków 1985, p. 62. (Galicia) in royal and monastic lands taken over by the state112. In the closest vicinity of Nowy Sącz (within its current borders) such a colony was established in 1785 in Dąbrówka, on the land confiscated from the estate of the Norbertines of Nowy Sącz. Initially, it was intended for Jews (it was then called New Jerusalem), but eventually German colonists settled there, which in 1788 was reflected in the name Deutsch Dąbrówka113. Its main axis was today’s Grunwaldzka Street. Plots with houses and farm buildings were laid out perpendicularly to it, and they were enclosed on each side by roads – today’s Zielona and Zawiszy Czarnego Streets114. At a similar time, former Hungarian Suburb, where in the 1780s land was bought by German immigrants, was regulated; in 1808 houses of fifty-one German colonists were recorded there115. The layout of this colony had already been largely obliterated (perhaps never fully delineated?) by the middle of the 19th century. Taking the 1846 cadastral map as a basis for a hypothetical reconstruction, we may assume that this large colony consisted of two sets of residential plots: a smaller one with one line of buildings on the north side of Grodzka Street, and a larger one, with two lines of buildings situated on either side of the main axis of the estate, i.e. today’s Długosza Street, delineated parallel to the “Hungarian” tract (today’s Jagiellońska Street). Its eastern line, bounded at the back by a road (also plotted in a straight line) corresponding to the present Jan Matejki Street, is still legible today, while the western line has been mostly absorbed by the later urban park (see below). The third colony within the current town boundaries was Laufendorf (1786) in Biegonice, a village taken away from the Poor Clares of Stary Sącz monastery. A complex of several houses at Elektrodowa and Towarowa Streets as well as the site of the former Protestant church have been preserved there116. A fourth colony, Hundsdorf, was created in 1786 at the border of Nowy Sącz, next to the manor in Chełmiec, which was also confiscated from the Poor Clares of Stary Sącz117.

Architectural transformations have changed the image of Nowy Sącz. It was described as an orderly and carefully developed town already in 1809 by Austrian official and traveller Samuel Bredetzky118. In the centre of the town only brick buildings (apart from outbuildings) were allowed to be erected in accordance with fire safety rules, although isolated wooden houses, probably as a legacy of the era of destruction, still existed in the middle of the 19th century even near the market square. Compact buildings of medieval and modern origin have been subject to thorough rebuilding and renovation, with the introduction of Baroque-Classicist and Classicist forms. In the suburbs, as in other Galician towns at the time, e.g. in Tarnów, a Classicist manor house became a characteristic building. With its single-storey form, high roof and often columned portico, it was reminiscent of the country houses of the nobility. Public buildings were erected, although the needs of the Austrian authorities in this respect were largely satisfied by the rebuilding of the castle120 (it was rebuilt according to a cost estimate drawn up in 1784 by the official builder, Loebzöltern, after the western part fell into the Dunajec as a result of a flood in 1813, converted into barracks in 1838, then into a prison) and confiscated monastery buildings. In 1834, the Renaissance town hall underwent reconstruction in the Classicist style. A military post was placed in the town hall and a guardhouse in the added column portico. The hospital building was erected in 1827121 on the site of today’s “school” church; the building of the municipal mess was constructed at a similar time at 18 Jagiellońska Street (today thoroughly rebuilt). The original forms of both these buildings are known from views of 1878122.

The effects of the anti-monastic policy of the Austrian authorities were clearly visible. Already in 1785, the authorities took over the Franciscan complex, moving the monks to Stary Sącz (from where they were expelled after less than half a century). In 1789, almost entire Gothic church was demolished. One of the retained buildings was the Baroque chapel of the Transfiguration, which in 1801–1803, together with the monastery buildings, was adapted to the needs of the Protestant community founded at that time (1803), catering for German-speaking migrants123; the former chapel has retained its function as an Protestant church to the present day. The Piarist monastery, which was dissolved by an imperial decree in 1786, underwent rebuilding in 1818 as a grammar school and finally, in 1855, as a prison, which is still there today; the church was demolished124. The abolition of monasteries and religious congregations was accompanied by support for parish churches. In Nowy Sącz, this was reflected in the thorough reconstruction of St. Margaret’s Church (1807–1822). At that time, the two-nave division of the body was removed in favour of a spacious interior. The facades were completely transformed. The effects of these measures lasted until the 1950s–1970s. The considerable scope of work was probably connected with the above-mentioned intention to establish a bishopric in Nowy Sącz. From the 1780s, small churches in the suburbs – St. Adalbert, St. Valentine, St. Cross – were liquidated. The latter was used as a powder magazine during the Napoleonic wars and was demolished around 1830126. The Church of St. Nicholas has been preserved, and in the course of the extension of 1844 it acquired its present late-Classicist form. From the end of the 18th century, the church had a cemetery. The location of the cemetery outside the town centre – with the simultaneous liquidation of the medieval cemetery at the former collegiate church – was in line with the sanitary policy of the Austrian authorities127. Mills were still operating on the Kamienna River millstreams and new ones were being built. At the end of the 18th century, there was a sawmill operating in the area of the intersection of today’s Królowej Jadwigi and Klasztorna Streets, and in the first half of the 19th century, a mill was built next to it. In 1843, the Jesuits from Nowy Sącz constructed a mill128, preserved – after reconstructions and extensions in the second half of the century – until today. The water to the millstream connected to this and two other mills marked on the cadastral plan of 1846 was directed by a weir, obliquely crossing the riverbed above the bridge called “Na Piekle” (“On Hell”). The number of inhabitants of Nowy Sącz was systematically increasing and their ethnic composition was also changing129. In the 1770s, the town counted more than 2.2 thousand inhabitants; the majority – about 80% – were Poles of the Roman Catholic faith, and about 19% were Jews. On the threshold

of the self-government era (Autonomy of Galicia), in the years 1857–1867, the number of inhabitants increased to 7.5–8.1 thousand; Jews already made up more than 30% of the population. With the development of the colony and the influx of officials from Austria-Hungary, a German-speaking population arrived, as well as Czechs and Hungarians. Protestants – mainly German-speaking – lived mainly in colonies outside the town; in Nowy Sącz alone their number until the 1830s probably did not exceed 200, which constituted less than 4.5% of the then 4.5 thousand population. urbanistic and architectural transformation of the town in the era of the autonomy of galicia (1866–1918) The reform of the Austrian state, as a result of which Galicia gained autonomy and municipalities in the whole province gained self-government, influenced positively the fundamental urbanistic and architectural transformations, characteristic for Galician towns, including Nowy Sącz. In 1866, the local government was established (municipal council – magistrate headed by the mayor)130. Earlier, in 1850, the state administration was reorganised, replacing the Kreis system with county offices. Nowy Sącz became a county city, included in the Act of 1889 among thirty large cities in Galicia131. During the period of Autonomy, there was a significant increase in the number of inhabitants: from 9.3 thousand (1869) to almost 25 thousand (1914). The vast majority were Poles (of the Roman Catholic faith). On the eve of World War I, there were 8 thousand Jews (31.8%), 367 Protestants (mainly German-speaking; less than 1.5%) and 296 Greek Catholics (1.2%)132. The character of the development was determined by resolutions of the city council133. A resolution from 1870 divided the space of Nowy Sącz into three zones. According to its provisions, in the central zone, corresponding essentially to the medieval town, “all buildings are to be of hard material”; in the next zone, comprising essentially historical suburbs, “residential buildings must be of brick”; and in the outer zone no such restrictions applied. The city fire of 1894 had a significant impact on urbanistic regulation and the formation of brick buildings. During the period of reconstruction, Lviv engineer Marcin Maślanka developed a geodetic survey135; it was used to delineate roads, regulate streets, install sewage systems, lay pavements. An important urban novelty in the Old Town was Trzeciego Maja Square (May 3rd)136, laid out between 1898 and 1903 on the site of some disused plots delineated during the foundation of the town. In fact, it was only as a result of reconstruction after the fire that the last single-storey houses, sketched by Stanisław Wyspiański back in 1889, disappeared from the market square137. In 1903, after a five-year effort (since 1898), the area of Nowy Sącz was extended by the incorporation of Zakamienica (called Piekło) and Załubińcze138, whereas the following year, the city’s central zone was considerably extended. The new district was connected to the medieval town by reinforced concrete bridges over the Kamienica: in 1904, by means of the extension of Tarnowska Street, whereas in 2019–2021 – Lwowska Street. In 1904, the construction of the municipal water supply system was commenced under the direction of the outstanding water engineering specialist, Roman Kajetan Ingarden of Cracow. The water intake in Świniarsk and the water reservoir in Gołąbkowice were designed by Kazimierz Górski, an engineer. At the same time, the city’s sewage system was being built according to a design by engineer Fryderyk Pordes; the water and sewage system was put into operation between 1910 and 1911139. Almost at the same time, between 1911 and 1912, the building of the municipal power station on the Żeglarka stream was built, designed by Cracovian architect Jerzy Struszkiewicz. It produced alternating current (three-phase) from a diesel dynamo. A similar technique, new in Galicia at the time, was only used at power stations in Lviv and Cracow140.

The connection of Nowy Sącz to the railway network contributed to the development of the city. The so-called Tarnów– Leluchów railway line, on the route from Tarnów to Budapest, completed in 1876, ran along the edge of the city141. The course of this road, formerly a dirt track adapted for this purpose, is echoed by present Stefan Batory Avenue and Wolności (Liberty) Avenue, which in the 20th century became one of the city’s most important arteries. In 1884, another line of the Podkarpacie Transversal Railway was built through Nowy Sącz. It played an important role in the state defence strategy143; the Nowy Sącz Miasto station was built on it. Thanks to the connection of the two lines, Nowy Sącz became an important transport hub, with a steam locomotive depot and railway repair workshops. These workshops belonged to the most important industrial plants in Galicia. They were built in the years 1876–1886 thanks to Sącz inhabitant, Karol Kwolewski144. A new social and professional group which emerged in the city was railway workers. They inhabited a modern housing estate built for them, the so-called railway colony145. The project of the colony was drawn up in Vienna in 1891 and carried out from the following year until the outbreak of the First World War; the works were supervised by Juliusz Miszke, a builder from Sącz146. The plan of the colony was based on a regular chequer layout, with standardised plots, detached brick houses and farm buildings147. Already in the first year of construction, thirty-seven of the one hundred planned houses were completed. In 1901, the city council passed a resolution to connect the railway colony with Świętej Kunegundy Street. The development of the colony (later known as the Old Colony) continued during the First World War; along with the construction of more houses in 1917, a medical clinic and a bathhouse were added148. The versatility of Nowy Sącz architecture154 after 1894 almost equalled the main Galician cities of Cracow and Lviv. The historic centre of the city and the areas directly adjacent to it were dominated by tenement houses, oneor rarely two-storey buildings, which gave Nowy Sącz its “big-city” character155. Single-storey houses with gardens and villas were built in the suburbs. An interesting villa housing estate has been built in Wólki. The image of the city resulted from the investment boom, but the involvement of architects from Cracow and Lviv (Teodor Talowski, Karol Knaus, Teodor Hoffmann, Jerzy Struszkiewicz, Wincenty Rawski jr, Jan Stobiecki) should also be appreciated. They were accompanied by the local community of architects and builders, with the leading representative, Zenon Adam Remi (1873–1924)156, who became a city planner (from 1903) after Karol Schmiedehausen, Stanislaw Eljasz-Radzikowski and Jan Peroś. This graduate of the Imperial and Royal State Industrial School in Lviv started his professional career in Cracow. In his numerous projects (24 public buildings and 30 residential houses), he presented an easily recognisable and original style, alluding to a picturesque Historicism. Particularly noteworthy are the architectural accents he introduced. The former Węgierska Street, renamed to Jagiellońska in 1884, became a representative arterial road. At the turn of the 19th and 20th centuries, numerous magnificent public buildings were constructed in this street – the seat of the Advance Money Fund (No. 8, architect Zenon Adam Remi, 1906–1907), the women’s department school (No. 32, engineer Julian Miszke, 1894–1897), the seat of the starosty office (No. 33, architect Jan Peroś, 1905–1907), the Municipal Savings Bank (No. 26, architect Karol Knaus, 1892–1893), the Treasury Directorate (No. 52, architect Wincenty Rawski jr, 1899), a branch of the Austro-Hungarian Bank (No. 56, architect Teodor Hoffmann, 1911–1912), the “Imperial” hotel (No. 14, architect Stanisław Eliasz, 1895). Equally impressive were the neighbouring tenement houses: No. 3 (architects Julian Niedzielski, 1895), No. 5 and 22 (architect J. Peroś, 1894–1895, 1908), No. 7, 11, 12, 17, 19, 27, 48 (architect Z. A. Remi, 1897– 1912), No. 16 (architect Szczęsny Zaremba, c. 1891), No. 30 (architect Józef Wojtyga, 1911–1912). The seat of the “Sokół” Gymnastic Society and the men’s department school (architect J. Peroś, 1894–1898) were built on Długosza Street (engineer Witold Żebracki, 1892; extension by architect J. Wojtyga, from 1913)158. The seat of the District Court was located on Pijarska Street (Wiktor Budzyński and Marian Litwa, 1899–1903)159, new hospital – on Młyńska Street (architects Adolf Kamieniobrodzki from Lviv, 1904–1908), whereas new military barracks – at 1. Pułku Strzelców Podhalańskich Street (1901–1906). The most important buildings of this period include the new Art Nouveau railway station (1909, interior decorated with paintings by Edmund Cieczkiewicz in 1911)160.

The Galician phase of Nowy Sącz’s history ended with World War I. Despite the brief occupation by Russian troops in 1914194 and the heavy fighting that took place in its area, the city was left unscathed, apart from the railway bridge on the Dunajec, which was damaged195. Spatial and architectural transformations in the Second Polish Republic: 1918–1939 In 1918, Nowy Sącz became part of the reborn Polish state as a district city in the Kraków Voivodeship. The conditions for its development in the interwar period were closely linked to the situation of Poland at the time. It was characterised by two main phases. Firstly (1918–1925/1930), while building the new state, an attempt was made to maintain civilisational and cultural continuity with the period preceding the First World War. The destruction and impoverishment caused by the war and the long struggle for borders and sovereignty (Silesian uprisings, Polish-Soviet war in 1920) made it a challenging task; ultimately, this phase was ended by the great world economic crisis of the late 1920s and early 1930s. The aim of the second phase (1935–1939) was to overcome the economic crisis by intensively modernising Poland, taking advantage of the development of industry and technology (including the construction of the sea port in Gdynia and the Central Industrial District – abbreviated in Polish as COP), state loans and modern banking (the National Economy Bank – BGK). A new way of management was also applied, based on the idea of regionalism as a method of stimulating and exploiting local opportunities of particular areas (regions) of Poland. Considering the developmental phases of the interwar period thus outlined196, it should be noted that in the first of these, Nowy Sącz continued the Galician tradition of a well-organised 192 Por. The population of the city grew from over 26,000 (1921) to 34,000 on the eve of the Second World War. Ethnically, as in the Galician era, Poles of Roman Catholic faith predominated, whereas Jews made up about 30% of the population. Spatial planning processes in the first phase of the interwar period were limited to the implementation of new buildings or small building complexes. Residential housing was a priority199. It was typical for Nowy Sącz that the villas far outnumbered the few tenement houses. Two styles of villas were predominant: Historicist and Modernist “manor style”. Two working-class housing estates were built: the so-called New Railway Colony, with two-storey houses, adjacent to the railway workshops in the south, in the area of 29 Listopada and Wyspiańskiego Streets, and another one on Henryka Sienkiewicza Street. An intensive development of Załubińcze, consisting mainly of villas and single-family houses, took place along the streets laid out here, including Jana Kochanowskiego Street. Numerous houses, surrounded by greenery, were built on plots of land along the newly delineated Zielona Street in Dąbrówka Niemiecka. The new architecture was largely the work of local builders, such as Walenty Cyło, Józef Wojtyga200 Zenon Marian Remi (son of Zenon Adam Remi), Zygmunt Słaby, Józef Koula, Michał Jastrzębski. As far as the sacral architecture is concerned, the “railway” church was extended in 1930–1931 under the direction of arch. Szczepan Sławiński. In 1937, its patron saint, St. Elisabeth, was replaced by the Patrocinium of the Sacred Heart of Jesus and the church was turned into a parish church201. This was yet another reorganisation of the parish network in Nowy Sącz, involving the separation of the Parish Church of St. Roch in Dąbrówka Polska from its mother parish of St. Margaret. This occurred as a result of the aforementioned division of Dąbrówka, part of which – Dąbrówka Niemiecka – was incorporated into the city in 1923. The Parish Church of St. Margaret and the “school” Church of St. Casimir were decorated with paintings by Jan Bukowski202. The end of 1927 saw the establishment of the Committee for the Development of Nowy Sącz. In 1930, the work on the zoning plan started, but it was not finalised until the outbreak of the war. At first, the work was supervised by one of the most outstanding Polish city planners, architect Ignacy Drexler, professor of the Lviv Technical University. It was then that the concept of forming a new city centre was adopted, which was to develop (in accordance with earlier tradition) towards the south. In 1935, the construction of President Mościcki Avenue (now Wolności / Liberty Avenue) began, delineated as an extension of Stefan Batory Street, reaching the city park – Planty. Thus, the decision of the city council, which was enacted back in 1905, was implemented208. At the same time, an axis was initiated for the future new Centrum district, which was created on this site after the Second World War. Architect Zbigniew Wzorek, a native of Nowy Sącz and later a professor at the Cracow University of Technology, took part in designing the avenue209. The new arterial road was planned as a representative axis connecting the railway station with the historic centre of the city. New streets, such as Szczęsnego Morawskiego and Stefana Żółkiewskiego, were laid out perpendicular to it.

As mentioned before, in the 1930s, the idea of regionalism played an important role in the development of Nowy Sącz. It sought to highlight the city’s identity through environmental, historical, demographic and cultural factors. Promotion of the regional specificity was enhanced, among others, by the Mountain Feast organised in Nowy Sącz by the Union of Mountain Lands in 1938, and also by choosing the city to host an elite military unit – the 1st Regiment of Podhale Rifles216. In 1939, a reputable regional magazine began to be published – “Rocznik Sądecki”217. Important for strengthening the city’s identity was the restoration in 1938 of the historical coat of arms with St. Margaret, instead of the Galician coat of arms with the knight218. Restoration of monuments also progressed219, involving in particular the restoration and partial reconstruction of the castle, initiated by a committee set up in 1926220. The castle was intended to become the seat of the Museum of the Sącz Region, established in 1938. The restoration works, supported by Mayor Władysław Barbacki, involved numerous representatives of the local community, including architects Remi, Cyło and Wojtyga, and well-known Cracow architects, Prof. Adolf Szyszko-Bohusz and mainly Zygmunt Gawlik. 212 L. (Dzieje niez­ During World War II, Nowy Sącz fell within the borders of the General Government. The occupying forces not only introduced the German name for the city, Neu Sandec, but also tried to imbue it with a German character. They systematically destroyed the Polish culture, liquidated monuments testifying to the patriotism of its inhabitants, such as monuments to Adam Mickiewicz and Władysław Jagiełło (the statue of the king was saved) and the Tomb of the Unknown Soldier (today reconstructed in the municipal cemetery). The German administration221 completed some projects begun before the war, including the floodbanks and the dam on the Dunajec River at Rożnów, where a hydroelectric power station producing electricity for Nowy Sącz was opened in 1942. In 1942, the area of the city was extended to include Falkowa, Gołąbkowice, Chruślice, Roszkowice and part of Chełmiec (Helena). As a result – and especially as a result of the deportations of the Polish population from Greater Poland, Pomerania and Silesia carried out by the occupying authorities in 1939/1940 – the number of inhabitants (before the Holocaust) increased by about 10,000 people, to over 43,000, as displaced refugees flowed into Nowy Sącz.

Polish residents of Nowy Sącz and the region were subjected to persecution. There were labour camps in the city, e.g. in the area of the so-called railway garden (from the end of 1942 until autumn 1944)222. The occupiers committed many executions on the streets and in isolated places (in the brickyard in Biegonice223, Rdziostów224, at the foot of the railway embankment by the bridge over the Dunajec River, on the road bridge over the Kamienica river). The house at 13 Czarnieckiego Street, the seat of the Gestapo, gained a grim reputation225. The most severe losses were suffered by the Jews of Nowy Sącz. The Holocaust entailed the murder of 11,500 Jews from Nowy Sącz in Nazi death camps; over a thousand people died in Nowy Sącz226. Between 1941 and 1943, 18,000 Jews from Nowy Sącz and the surrounding areas – Stary Sącz, Grybów, Bobowa, Krynica – as well as those from other places further, were crowded into two separate ghettos, which operated from August 1941 to July 1942. After the brutal pacification, in which most of the victims were deported to the Belzec death camp, the buildings of the inner-city ghetto were ruined; the synagogue was destroyed and profaned. Executions often took place in the profaned Jewish cemetery; matzevots were used to build pavements. Next to the cemetery the occupants arranged a market. As a result of the warfare of the time, three bridges collapsed (only the bridge over the Kamienica along Lwowska Street survived). urban development during the Polish People’s Republic: 1945–1989 After the Second World War, the Polish legal order from before the occupation was restored. Nowy Sącz once again became a district city in the Kraków Voivodeship. The administrative structures of the Polish state evolved and in 1951 the city gained the status of a city district. Then, as a result of the national administration reform of 1975, which abolished districts and introduced a new division into provinces (voivodeships), Nowy Sącz province was created; the city became its capital. This state of affairs lasted until 1996, when as a result of another reform, districts were restored and Nowy Sacz, again as a city with district rights, found itself in the Lesser Poland Voivodeship.

Nowy Sącz, devastated by the occupation and war, had 22.6 thousand inhabitants in 1945, i.e. 37% fewer than at the end of the interwar period. This was the result of both the Holocaust and migration to the so-called Western Territories. Over time, the population increased steadily to 37,400 in 1965 and 75,000 in 1988228. The size of the urban territory has also changed. In the post-war period, the outlying villages of Chruślice (1951) and Falkowa (1969) were excluded from the urban limits (2425 ha). Later on, the tendencies were reversed: in 1973 parts of Biegonice, Dabrówka and Zawada were incorporated into Nowy Sącz, along with the remaining parts of these villages (in 1977), followed again Chruślice and Falkowa, as well as fragments of several other suburban villages: Wielopole, Zabełcze, Naściszowa, Piątkowa, Jamnica, Poręba Mała, Świniarska and Chełmiec. The effect of these changes was an enlargement of the city’s area to 5,706 ha, which has remained the same until today (2022)229. 227 L. After the war, the intention to develop a zoning plan for the city was revived231. The preparation of materials for this task was undertaken in the years 1946–1948 by architect Zbigniew Wzorek. After the war, he returned to Nowy Sącz and continued his work on pre-war President Mościcki Avenue (whose name was changed to Wolności /Liberty Avenue under the new political conditions). A new city centre district was to be created between the Old Town to the north and the industrial, warehousing and railway areas to the south. The project also included the construction of a National Remembrance Monument, dedicated to the victims of Second World War. The monument was located in the vicinity of the old cemetery by Church of St. Nicholas. Earlier, in 1945, a mausoleum of Soviet soldiers was established on Wolności Avenue (moved in 2015 to the municipal cemetery232).

However, the most urgent task was to remove the wartime damage; the city lost almost two hundred buildings233. Post-war reconstruction works were managed by the Municipal Reconstruction Bureau under the supervision of the Municipal Reconstruction Committee234. Based on the plan of reconstruction of the “Castle district”, prepared by Józef Wojtyga and Stanisław Ciechanowski, a complex of detached two-storey houses surrounded by greenery was built in 1950 on the site of the ruined Jewish quarter. Earlier, in the years 1947–1948, bridges over the Dunajec River (Krakowska Street) and over the Kamienica River (Tarnowska Street) were rebuilt. The first general zoning plan of Nowy Sacz was prepared in 1950–1953 in the Voivodeship Urban Planning Studio in Cracow (the assumptions were drawn up by S. Ciechanowski). For the purposes of this plan, the “Preliminary historical study of Nowy Sącz” was prepared, in which for the first time preservationist guidelines were set out, recognising Nowy Sącz as tche monument requiring protection, which would involve the elimination of transit traffic through the Old Town district235. The plan envisaged population growth to 70,000 by 1970 and industrial development (Railway Repair Plant, Fruit Processing Plant). It was assumed that the population of the historic centre would stabilise, with development areas concentrated – in line with pre-war trends and the Central District concept – in the southern part of the city. The plan was developed amidst the liquidation of the municipal government and private enterprises, which were nationalised. In 1954, the importance of Wolności Avenue as the new city centre was emphasised by placing the sculpture of “Pietà Sądecka” (by Janina Reichert-Toth, Friedrich Toth) in the Monument of National Remembrance237. In 1957–1959, the second general zoning plan was created: “Perspective and stage plan of Nowy Sącz for the years 1960– 1965” (by Janina Knaus-Grygorowicz from the Regional Urban Planning Studio in Cracow), approved in 1959. It referred to the concept of the plan from 1950–1953 and was further developed in detailed plans which were prepared in the “Miastoprojekt” in Cracow and its subsidiary in Nowy Sącz, operating from 1959 under the direction of Andrzej Benedyktowicz and later Lech Skirzyński. The guiding idea of the general zoning plan was to develop separately the individual belts of the city; a new section of buildings was to use the area of Załubińcze, separated from the centre not only by the Kamienica river, but also by the greenery on the riverbank which was to be turned into a recreational and sports area. At the same time, appreciating the landscape values of Nowy Sącz, the plan assumed the protection of the panorama of the city from the east, from Zabełcka Mountain (from the Tarnów road), and from the west, from the winding roads to Limanowa and Cracow238. The panoramas were to be enriched by restoring height accents (helmets on the towers of the Sącz monuments)239. The arrangements of the zoning plan were implemented under special conditions provided by the so-called Sącz Experiment, initiated in 1958 (shortly after the October 1957, the political liberalisation of the state-wide politics) and formally concluded in 1975, but practically lasting only until 1964240. The experiment involved the introduction of a form of management that was unique in Poland at that time, which enabled the district and city of Nowy Sącz – as the only area in the People’s Republic – to be exempt from the rules of a centrally planned economy in favour of economic independence. It was to be based on the exploitation and development of local spa, holiday and tourist capacities, the stimulation of local industry and crafts and the development of fruit and vegetable processing241. Between 1976 and 1977, the population of Nowy Sącz increased from 48.6 to 59.5 thousand people. In 1990, the city was to have 100,000 inhabitants, and this growth was to provide a workforce for the expanding industry. The industry was to develop primarily in the southern part of the city (from Biegonice to Gorzków), but also in the northern and western parts (part of Świniarsk, Chełmiec, Helen). The Sącz Car Repair Works was established at 144 Węgierska Street (1979). Modernisation also involved the railway: in 1986 electric traction replaced steam. A symbol of change was the restoration in 1989 of the city’s pre-war coat of arms with the patron saint252. The assumed rate of development required an increase in housing construction. According to the plan, this was to be achieved by building new housing estates with multi-storey blocks of flats. As a result, as early as 1977, the construction of such a housing estate began in Gołąbkowice (Barskie IIA). By the end of the 1980s, several more were built: Barskie IIB, Wojska Polskiego, Gorzków I and Gorzków II. They changed the architectural and urban landscape of the city. In the 1980s, a trend emerged to abandon the construction of “scattered” blocks of flats, including those made of large panels, in favour of building up street interiors using traditional technologies. One example is a small housing estate in Gorzków, in the area of Konstanty Klemens Gucwa Street, designed by Jerzy Osowiński (Voivodeship Design Office in Nowy Sącz) in 1983 and put into use five years later. The confrontation of the Communist totalitarian state with the Church prevented the construction of new churches for a long time. Still in 1949, it was possible to divide the Sącz church organisation into two deaneries: Nowy Sącz Północ and Nowy Sącz Południe. To meet the religious needs of the growing population, a new parish was established at the Church of the Holy Spirit in 1950. The October 1956 political breakthrough in Poland made it possible to build churches on a very limited scale. In this early period, only one church was built in Nowy Sącz – the Church of Our Lady of Sorrows in Zawada, designed by Tadeusz Brzoza of Zakopane, with work commencing in 1957 and continuing until 1981. New parishes were established at existing churches: in 1964 at St. Casimir’s Church (so far a rector’s church), in 1967 at the White Immaculate Convent, in 1980 at St. Helena’s Church. Building investments only took place after the “Solidarity” uprising of 1980. Churches were built for the new parishes: Church of Our Lady of the Immaculate Conception in the Millenium estate in the Kamienica valley (designed by Leszek Filar and his team, 1982–1992), Church of the Holy Cross in the Helena district behind the Dunajec (designed by Zenon Trzupek, 1984), Church of the Holy Trinity in Dąbrówka Polska (designed by Paweł Dygoń, 1988) and Church of Our Lady of Czestochowa in Zabełcze (designed by Paweł Dygoń, 1989). In 1983, the Calvary of Nowy Sącz was established – a large sacral and landscape complex in Leśna Street in the Chruślice housing estate. The network of cemeteries has also expanded: new municipal cemeteries were established in Biegonice, in Węgierska Street (1994) and in Dąbrówka Polska, in Ruczaj Street (2000).

Thanks to the efforts of the provincial conservator in Cracow – Hanna Pieńkowska – and the local city authorities, the monuments of Nowy Sącz were effectively protected during the difficult Communist era253. Immediately after the war, the ruined remains of the castle were saved from destruction, including the Blacksmiths’ Tower (designed by Stefan Świszczowski from Cracow). The former St. Margaret’s Collegiate Church has been extensively restored. The work was carried out in two stages: 1955–1969 – conservation of the facade and restoration of the differentiated height of the towers in the facade (designed by arch. Stefan Świszczowski); 1969–1973 – covering the interior with a modern shell vault, suggesting the original two-nave spatial arrangement (designed by arch. Józef T. Gawłowski of the Silesian University of Technology in Gliwice). The adjacent complex of former chapter houses was adapted to accommodate the District Museum (1960–1966, designed by Józef Ptak, Preservation of Monuments Workshop in Cracow). In the years 1962–1966, the post-Franciscan complex was reconstructed and the helmet crowning the tower was restored (Janusz Smólski, Preservation of Monuments Workshop in Cracow); as a result, an important accent in the city’s skyline was restored. The synagogue, destroyed by the Nazis, was adapted for museum purposes in 1971–1982. The Jewish cemetery, recovered by the religious community in 1948, was reconstructed: a fence was erected with tombstones shattered by the occupier (this motif, called the Wailing Wall, recurs in Jewish cemeteries after the Holocaust), Chaim Halberstam’s ohel was rebuilt (1946–1947), the mortal remains of the Jews from Stary Sącz and Limanowa – victims of Nazi execution – were buried here, and one and a half thousand matzevot used for paving roads were recovered and relocated here. The creation of the Nowy Sącz Ethnographic Park on the border of Gołąbkowice and Falkowa was a major success. The general programme principles were outlined by H. Pieńkowska. Work on this programme has been ongoing from 1962 in the Municipal Urban Planning Complex and the District Museum; the programme was detailed by Tadeusz Szczepanek, Director of the Museum, and the design was developed by Wojciech Szczygieł. The opening of the Ethnographic Park – as a branch of the Museum – took place in 1975254.

City planning and architectural transformations in the Third Polish Republic: 1990–2020 Nowy Sącz currently has a population of 84,000. Administratively, it is divided into twenty-five auxiliary units (housing estates), which correspond to the historical settlement units: Old Town with suburbs, 20th-century housing estates and former villages incorporated into the city. The spatial development of Nowy Sacz in the recent period is closely connected with the political and social breakthrough initiated in Poland by the elections of 1989, which led to the return of democracy and restoration of free market economy. By virtue of the Local Self-Government Act passed in 1990255, the city gained subjectivity and was able to adopt a new development strategy. Even before the liquidation of the Nowy Sącz Voivodeship, the latest “General plan of spatial development for the city of Nowy Sącz” was drawn up in 1996 by the City Planning Office under the direction of Maria Modzelewska of Nowy Sącz256. It presupposed the shaping of spatial order in a situation of dynamic development of the capital of the voivodeship, protection of the landscape by excluding development of the slopes of the hills surrounding the city, preservation of the Old Town complex and modernisation of roads (especially exit streets) while limiting transportation transit. The implementation of the last task started with the construction of the route over the łubinka River on the northern side of Nowy Sącz, used as a shortcut of the National Road No. 75 between Tarnów and Krynica bypassing the city centre. Its first section was Witosa Street, starting from the intersection with 253 H. At the same time, the bridge over the Kamienica River on Tarnowska Street was replaced by a new structure, which is still in place today.

The city administrators passed a programme entitled “Nowy Sacz – health and greenery” in 1996257. The programme included the following tasks to be carried out in subsequent years: the construction of a sewage treatment plant for the whole city in Wielopole (1996–2002/2006258), establishment of a municipal landfill in Zabełcze-Przetakówka (1998–2007259), construction of an indoor swimming pool and sports hall at 34 Nadbrzeżna Street (2002260), revitalisation of the Dunajec Rifle Park as a place of leisure and recreation (after 2014261), renovation and modernisation of street and pavement surfaces (since 2007). A manifestation of the growing importance of Nowy Sącz are the higher education institutions operating here, replacing the previous branches of Cracow universities. In 1991, the nonpublic Sącz-Podhale Business School was established. Two years later it was transformed into the National Louis University – Higher School of Business, highly ranked among Polish universities. In 1998, the State Higher Vocational School in Nowy Sacz was established262. The local government decided on changes in the management of urban infrastructure. The Building Combine in Zielona Street was liquidated; its facilities were taken over in 1993 by the aforementioned Higher School of Business. The Nowy Sącz Public Utilities Company ceased to exist, partially replaced in 1996 by the Municipal Heat Supply Company due to the development of the heating network263. Poland’s accession to the European Union in 2004 gave a new impulse to Nowy Sącz’s development. The city gained access to European funds through the so-called voivodeship contracts. Nowy Sącz was included in the Regional Operational Programme for the Małopolska Region, which is part of the National Cohesion Strategy. 257 M. Smoleń, Nowy Sącz w 1996 r., RS, vol. 25, 1997, p. 260. 258 Ibidem, p. 328. The construction of the sewage treatment plant was part of a major expansion of the water and sewage network covering Nowy Sącz and the nearby municipalities: Stary Sącz, Nawojowa and Kamionka Wielka, funded by the European Union, which lasted until 2015. Cf. L. Migrała, Historia…, p. 423. In 2007, the urban layout of the Old Town in Nowy Sącz was entered into the register of monuments264. The preservation conditions that must be taken into account in the spatial development plans prepared in accordance with the 2003 Act have been clearly defined265. Legal protection of historical monuments was introduced already in “Study of the conditions and directions of spatial development of Nowy Sącz”, which was passed in 2008 (and amended in 2011 and 2017266). The recommendations of the “Study of the conditions” are consistent with several other plans: “Concept of the spatial development of the country until 2030”, “Strategy of the development of the Lesser Poland Voivodeship for 2011–2020”, “Plan of the spatial development of the Lesser Poland Voivodeship” and “Strategy of the development of City of Nowy Sącz 2020+”267.

“Study of conditions” played an important role in shaping the spatial layout of the city. Assuming the maintenance and development of Nowy Sącz at the bottom of the Sącz Basin (leaving the slopes of the surrounding hills undeveloped), the need to improve the communication system in the city and its surroundings was indicated. Surrounding Nowy Sącz with two ring roads will supposedly protect the city against transit traffic. The ring roads were to be built as a result of construction or reconstruction of national roads and city streets. This task, still unfinished, is being implemented in stages. Outer ring road goes through city outskirts. The first stage of its construction is the so-called northern ring road, which was built in 2014–2015 as a westward extension of the route over the łubinka. The extension of this road starts from the new roundabout named after John Paul II (at the intersection of Tarnowska and Witosa Streets), runs through the flyover and the bridge over the Dunajec River268, and leads up to the western ring road (also opened in 2015269) running along the Dunajec River valley and connecting with National Road No. 28. The function of the eastern ring road is performed by Józef Piłsudski Avenue in the valley of the Kamienica River, which was modernised in 2007–2011. The southern ring road, i.e. the new connection of Józef Piłsudski Avenue with Węgierska Street and so-called Węgierska-Bis Street with a bridge over the Poprad River, leading to Stary Sącz, awaits completion. The inner, smaller ring of roads is designed around the city centre, involving existing and planned streets. In the most recent phase of the history of Nowy Sacz, the building movement has been significantly revived. As in many Polish cities, large supermarkets started to emerge: the first of these was “Real” (later “Auchan”) on the outskirts of Nowy Sącz in Gorzków (1999). Among the numerous (about 30) objects of this type, distinguished by their architectural splendour are the shopping mall “Sandecja” on Węgierska Street (opened in 2009; designed by the Design Agency A4 Marek Smaga and Partners from Nowy Sącz), the shopping mall “Gołąbkowice” on Lwowska Street (opened in 2011), the shopping, service and entertainment centre “Trzy Korony” at 80 Lwowska Street (built in 2011–2013, opened in 2013; designed by Marek Gachowski, ARCUS Design and Consulting Office in Gliwice). Od warsztatów do The fortifications of Nowy Sącz first aroused interest as early as the 19th century, when brief descriptions of them were published by Ż. Pauli, W. łuszczkiewicz, S. Tomkowicz, and the authors of the Geographical Dictionary of the Kingdom of Poland1. At the end of the nineteenth century and the beginning of the twentieth, the same topic was addressed by J. Sygański. Based on an analysis of modern written sources, he identified the location of the town gates and towers, at the same time crediting the construction of the walls to Casimir the Great2. In the following years, this topic remained a side issue for researchers, who as a rule linked the creation of the fortifications to the last of the crowned Piasts3. After the war, booklet no. 10 of the Catalogue of Monuments of Art of Poland, published in 1951 and devoted to Nowy Sącz poviat, includes a list of the surviving parts of the fortifications4. A major breakthrough came with a monograph published by J. Widawski, who summed up the state of research at that time and made many valuable comments of his own on the course, structure, appearance and chronology of the city walls of Nowy Sącz. He was the first researcher to suggest that they may have been built at the end of the 13th and the beginning of the 14th century, right after the town’s foundation, i.e. on the initiative of Wenceslaus II of Bohemia. The same researcher also suggested that the building work continued 1 Ż. Beiersdorf, who distinguished three phases in the functioning of the town walls in Nowy Sącz, dating their beginnings to the end of the 13th century6. The current state of knowledge about the fortifications in Nowy Sącz was recently recapitulated by P. Kocańda, who unambiguously dated their construction to the reign of Wenceslaus II of Bohemia7.

Only a few fragments of the old fortifications have survived up until the present day. In addition, the original material has been lost through numerous conservation efforts. The best-preserved section is located in the eastern part of the former defensive perimeter, in the presbytery garden, right behind the church of St. Margaret. This surviving fragment is 20 m long, roughly 5 m high (from the town side) and 1.4 m wide. At a height of 3.5 m, the structure juts outwards, supporting guard porch, and above it are crenellations with battlements. Św. Małgorzata Street (until 2018 known as Zakościelna), is a 40-meter section of the wall, reconstructed in 1918 and devoid of any original material. Another surviving fragment can be found in the southwest. corner of the Old Town, on the side of the Dunajec, more specifically behind the walls of the penitentiary (former Piarist monastery) at 12 Szwedzka Street. This is a small section of the fortifications with its accompanying buttress. The next section of the walls lies at the northern end of the town next to the ruins of the castle. It comprises the reconstructed Blacksmith›s Tower (in its Renaissance form) and a defensive wall, 8 metres in height and about 1.9 m thick. We can assume that a number of other unspecified sections have also survived in the walls of certain buildings as well as underground in the form of foundations. The fortifications of Nowy Sącz have hitherto not been archaeologically explored. However, remaining fragments have been discovered during various earthworks. In 1961, when digging sewage infrastructure on Wałowa Street, the foundations of the town walls were uncovered over a distance of 90 m together with a square tower. At that time, the discoveries were document, and the fragments were dismantled so that the earthworks could continue8. Selected fragments of these walls together with the foundations of the tower were rediscovered in 2013 during excavation work carried out in connection with the construction of the water supply network on Wałowa, along the section between Lwowska Street and Sobieski Street. The exposed tower was believed to be either the Furrier’s Tower or another tower, of unknown name, which protected the town from the side of the road to Grybów and Biecz. During these works, previously unidentified sections of the fortifications were also discovered, located at plot no. 94 and along tenement buildings 10 and 119. Until now, some parts of the defensive walls, located on a property on Wałowa Street, in the south-eastern section of the Old Town, have also survived up until the present. Nowy Sącz was founded on a flat elevation, at the fork of the rivers Dunajec (flowing from the west) and the Kamienica (located to the east). The waterways merge north of the town. From the east, west and north, the hill is cut off by steep slopes that defined the boundaries of the town and its fortifications. Only to the south was this area devoid of natural obstacles. The hill reached its highest point on a promontory on its northern part, where the castle itself was situated. Nowy Sącz’s strategic and defensive location was already being noted in the Middle Ages. The construction of the town walls began shortly after the city’s foundation in 1292 on the initiative of Wenceslaus II of Bohemia, who granted it extremely generous privileges and saw it as the main administrative and defensive centre beyond the Polish-Hungarian border. There are several arguments in favour of recognizing the Czech monarch as the founder of the fortifications. First of all, there exists one undated document in which the ruler exempted the townspeople from duties and tributes, provided that these funds were used to repair the walls muro­ rum ambitus, ubi indiquerit reparetur10. The act not only confirms the existence of the town’s fortifications as early as the end of the 13th century, but also tells us that the townspeople were expected to repair them. It can be assumed that the author of the “Rocznik Świętokrzyski” was referring to Nowy Sącz when he mentioned et alias municiones in Polonia12, apart from the fortifications of Cracow, as fortified works built on the initiative of the Czechs. This city is also missing from the lists of towns founded by Casimir the Great compiled by Jan of Czarnków and Jan Długosz, which according to some scholars indicates that its origins date from an earlier period13. This theory is also suggested by the political and social situation at that time as well as by an analysis of the structure of the oldest parts of the walls, which, to judge by the building technique used, resemble the Florian walls in Cracow and the first fortifications of Biecz14. In their initial form, the fortifications consisted of a defensive perimeter, three gates, square towers, as well as embankments and moats. The original walls were built of broken sandstone, connected with lime mortar, while maintaining equalizing layers. Their height is difficult to determine. According to J. Sygański, it was about 12 cubits (i.e. 7.20 8 m), while in the best-preserved section today it reaches a height of 5.5 m. The defensive walls were equipped with a guards’ walkway and battlement, the remains of which are nowadays visible in the eastern section. The defensive perimeter was adapted to the irregular form of the terrain layout and ran along the edge of the town’s escarpment. The total length was over 1.700 m. There were three gates along the line of fortifications, two main gates located on the N-S axis, i.e. the Cracow Gate (Porta Cracoviensis, from the north) and the Hungarian Gate (Porta Hungaricalis, from the south, erected 1488), while the third, the Mill Gate (Porta Molendinalis, erected 1368) was located in the south-east section, at the exit of the road leading to Grybów and Biecz. The actual appearance of the gatehouses is unknown, but it should be assumed that they took the form of square towers, protruding in front of the wall line and slightly higher than them. Also, they would have featured a passage and a drawbridge, similar to the Florian Gate in Krakow. During this period, the first towers may also have been built, as was reported by Jan Długosz. However, their form remains unclear. Based on analogies with Cracow’s (Pasamoników, Ciesielska) towers, it can be assumed that they were four-sided structures, equal in height to, or slightly higher than the defensive walls and open to the inside.

The construction work began during the reign of Wenceslaus II and was continued by his successors. Originally, only three curtains were erected, north, east and west, while from the south the town was devoid of brick fortifications, but the area was cut off by a deep moat and embankment15. Evidence for this can be found in a document of Władysław the Elbow-high from 1331, when, after the town fire, the ruler issued grants to the townspeople of Nowy Sącz, including permission to collect wood from forests near Rytro, which was intended for the repair of fortifications. The phrase blancos appears here, which should be understood as wood and earth fortifications16. The work on the fortifications continued in the second half of the 14th century. In 1368, Casimir the Great allowed the townspeople to widen the Mill Gate17. By the end of the 14th century, the entire defensive perimeter was probably already complete. However, the condition of the fortifications was unsatisfactory, as in 1405 Władysław Jagiełło had already freed the merchants of Sącz from the obligation to pay duty in Czchów, on the condition that the money saved would be used to repair the towers, walls and moats18. In the following years, there were frequent references to the town walls (e.g., in a topographical context; in 1409, in connection with the foundation of the Premonstratensian monastery, the intra muros civitates nostrae Nova Sandecz was given; in 1412 there is mention of an extra muros garden)19.

Phase II (from the beginning of the 16th century up to the end of 17th century) Starting from the beginning of the 16th century, the defensive perimeter was further strengthened, mainly by improving the existing fortifications and adapting them for the use of firearms. All the gates were extended upwards and assumed the form of high towers with extra floors and equipped with arrow slits. Similar modernization work was also carried out on the towers themselves, which received an additional floor (weapons stores were built into the vaulted ground floors, while the upper floors featured fire stations) and closed from the town side. According to 17th-century sources, they were furnished with sloping roofs covered with shingles or tiles and crowned with knobs adorned with flags or wooden figures20. Sygański also states that the roofs of the towers had attics21. During this period, a fourth gate, known as the Grodzka Gate, was erected, which led from the town to the castle22. During the modernization of the fortifications in the 16th–17th centuries, the top of the defensive walls was also altered, as the original battlement and guards’ walkway were closed and covered with a shingled roof, a fact which was mentioned in 154323. The work carried out in this second phase was not limited solely to modernization tasks, as new additions were also made. While, as was mentioned above, square towers should be included in the first phase, towers with a semi-circular shape and adapted to the use of firearms, were erected in more modern times. The most important defence project in this period was the construction of a fortalice in front of the Hungarian Gate. This investment was in response to the threat posed by the Turks and was part of a wider program aimed at strengthening cities in the southern part of the country. As part of this campaign, in 1555 King Sigismund Augustus allocated revenues from ore stocks in Nowy Sącz to finance the modernization of the fortifications24. The fortification in front of the Hungarian Gate was built in the years 1555–1557. The town’s registers contain very detailed information about this project, for example on the monies spent on numerous bricklayers and stonemasons. The new defensive works probably assumed the form of an elongated bastion flanking the gateway.

A central feature of the fortification works carried out at that time was the removal of the main defensive line from the town. In Nowy Sącz, this function was now to be performed by the second line of walls, moats and earth embankments. The construction of these elements probably began in the late Middle Ages. The earth embankments, the remains of which have survived to this day in the western and south-eastern parts of the Old Town, were confirmed by sources in 1405 and 154325. More references to them can be found in 17th-century sources. In a survey dating from 1615, we learn that the embankments built at great cost and which the border town very much needed, were being destroyed by the grazing of cattle and other animals, which was strictly forbidden. In 1639, the councillors asked King Władysław IV Vasa to allocate half of all tax revenues to the repair of the town walls and ditches. Major works aimed at strengthening the earth embankments were carried out in the 1750s in connection with the threat posed by Swedish and Transylvanian troops as well as in response to the news of the conquest of the castle in Czorsztyn by the army of Aleksander Kostka Napierski26. The earth fortifications were probably repaired at this time, and the moats were deepened. The construction of the second line of walls began in the second half of the 15th century, but the first written records date from more recent times, when it was referred to as a ‘fence’, a ‘low wall’, a ‘wall’, or a ‘small wall’. It certainly existed from the south side, where the line of the wall ran along the outer side of the embankment 23 J. Sygański, Historya…, vol. I, p. 215. 24 Z. Beiersdorf, B. Phase III (from the beginning of the 17th century up until the end of the 19th century) The works related to the Swedish invasion and the subsequent reconstruction of the fortifications brought to an end the period of modernization of the town fortifications in Nowy Sącz. In the following years, efforts were made to keep them in proper condition, for example, in 1671, the starost allocated a tenon tax for the renovation of the walls28. In the 18th century, the fortifications of Nowy Sącz were already visibly damaged and neglected. Due to advances in the art of war, they also ceased to perform their basic function. They even slowly began to interfere with the spatial development of the town. In 1712, a fire partially destroyed the Hungarian Gate. Some of the towers were turned into apartments, while the walls were demolished and used as materials for other buildings. In the lists of the town hall from 1786 we can find information that the defensive wall from the side of the Dunajec was in such a bad condition that it was in danger of collapsing. After the Second Partition, the Austrian authorities began to systematically dismantle the fortifications along with three town gates and the fortress. The demolition works lasted until 1804, but the remaining parts of the fortifications, including the Pottery Tower, were still in place until 182429. Until the end of the 19th century, some of the earth elements – a moat and an embankment – were still in existence, and these were eventually levelled during the expansion of the city. The final draft of the Mieg’s map (i.e. the topographic map of Galicia, 1779–1782) features an outline of the modern earthen fortifications planned by the Austrians in the 1870s in the wake of their conflict with Prussia. These fortifications, which were meant to be of a field, makeshift nature, consisted of two defense perimeters, further reinforced with redoubts. Nevertheless, such investment was never realized30. The non-existent court of Cracow bishops was located in the south-western part of the chartered town and was later called the Biskupie (nowadays this area is occupied by a prison). The origins of the residential building have not been explained so far, and no archaeological research has been carried out here. In the literature on the subject, the issue has been most extensively discussed by J. Sygański, B. Krasnowolski and Z. Beiersdorf, while P. Kocańda has provided the most recent recapitulation of the

According to some researchers, the establishment’s roots date back to the time before the town received its charter. Bishop Paweł of Przemanków supposedly begun its construction after 1280. The court not only served a defensive and residential function, but above all functioned as the center of the estate’s administration32. A more popular belief is that the construction of the residence took place after the town received its charter and was the initiative of Jan Muskata, a supporter of Wenceslaus II of Bohemia33. There are more arguments in favour of the latter theory. The appearance of the medieval bishop’s court is unknown. We know a great deal about the later history of the building. In the early 16th century, it was expanded in the Gothic-Renaissance style. In 1507, Master Thomas carpentarius de Novo Sandecz worked on its reconstruction. In a letter to the town council of Bardejów, he boasted about his work in curia Domini Episcopi in Sandecz34. This is the first mention of the bishop’s court. The works were carried out in the years 1507–1515; unfortunately the renovated building burned down in 1522. Renovation work were carried out again under the episcopate of Piotr Tomicki, but it was not enough, because in the second half of the 16th century the residence was already falling into ruin. In the following years, attempts were made to save the dilapidated court, but to no avail. The bishop’s inspection from 1608 indicates that the building was already in ruins and only the brick foundations and two vaulted cellars remained, as well as an impressive entrance gate with rich stonework details. Adjoining the residence were the town walls with two towers. All that stood on this site in the following years was a square with a garden called Biskupie, as was mentioned in 1652. The area was acquired by the Poor Clares, who started the construction of a new monastery here. Eventually, in 1732, the area was acquired by the Piarists, who brought a monastery and the church of St. Jan Kalasanty, which was in use until the dissolution of the order in 178635.

The royal castle in Nowy Sącz was located in the north-west. part of the town, on a headland at the fork of the Dunajec and Kamienica rivers. Currently, only small, neglected ruins have survived, while the rest of the complex is occupied by the municipal park. The origins of the stronghold have not been adequately explained. The remaining buildings were wooden structures serving residential and utility functions. However, the existence of a tenement type brick house cannot be ruled out. As the years passed, Sącz castle increased in importance as an important royal residence. Casimir the Great, who often visited Nowy Sącz, embarked on a major expansion of the complex. The work probably continued in the second half of the 14th century, during the reigns of the Anjous and Władysław Jagiełło. The first certified reference to its chapel dates to 1467. The stronghold, which took shape at that time, served as a royal lodge, hosting not only Polish rulers, but also foreign monarchs, including Emperor Sigismund of Luxembourg (in the years 1394, 1419 and 1424). According to tradition, the sons of Casimir IV Jagiellon, were also supposed to have lived in the castle under the care of Jan Długosz and Filip Buonaccorsi. Modern sources provide much more information about the castle. In 1522, it was consumed by a fire. The rebuilding of the residence was undertaken by the royal starosts, Piotr from Felsztyn and Jan Pieniążek from Krużlowa40. The first more detailed description dates from 1540, and tells us about the internal appearance and the layout of the rooms. At that time, the site already occupied a large area and was set apart from the town by a separate wall with a gate. Located in its vicinity was a stone well, next to which there were a new house and two cellars, used for food storage. In addition, there were other farm buildings in the courtyard (granaries, warehouses and stables, a kitchen, a drying room) and residential buildings (a room for a notary). Another survey carried out in 1569 informs us that the castle required extensive renovation work41. In the second half of the 16th century, the Nowy Sącz starosty was assigned to the

Lubomirski family. At that time, a major expansion of the castle was carried out, and it assumed the form of a magnate’s residence. Unfortunately, in 1611, it was destroyed by a fire. Over the next few years, Stanisław and Sebastian Lubomirski managed to rebuild the castle, and their efforts are precisely documented by surveys carried out in 1616 and 1627. They inform that it was surrounded by a wall with a Grodzka Gate and a wicket from the town side. Inside, it consisted of a huge residential building, partially with a basement, and housed forty rooms. From the north side, the Noble Tower adjoined the castle. The inner buildings were complemented by farm buildings42. 18th century sources show the building as being partially deserted and in need of urgent repairs. A review conducted in 1768 shows the residence destroyed by yet another fire, with most of the interior fittings, floors and ceilings burnt, the walls covered with numerous cracks, and the windowpanes missing43. After 1772, the castle and the starosty were handed to Józef Wielogłowski, from whom the Austrian government demanded that necessary renovation work be undertaken. Due to the fact that the castle’s custodians were reluctant to carry out repairs, the partitioning authorities took this task upon themselves. However, their efforts also proved ineffective, since in 1793 it was recorded in the official protocol that the starost’s castle was in danger of falling into total ruin. The final death blow came with the flood of 1813, as a result of which the western part of the castle collapsed. The remaining part of the stronghold was converted into barracks in 183844. Ten years later, the Austrian authorities sold the castle to the town, which at the time was still being used as a prison. In the following years, attempts were made to save the ruins, while in 1936 the collections of the Museum of the Sącz Region were placed here. STADT NEU SANDEC POLNISCH NOWY SACZ IN GALIZIEN SANDECER KREIS, 1846 Litografia wielobarwna, papier, 10 arkuszy, skala 1 : 2880 przeskalowany do 1 :25 000 i połączone sekcje. Miasto w granicach ówczesnych. Plan posiada bardzo czytelny układ działek miejskich i przedmiejskich z zaznaczonymi granicami własności, każda działka ma własny numer. Zabudowa ze zróżnicowaniem na murowaną (kolor czerwony), drewnianą (żółty), zaznaczono także tereny zielone. Widoczne dwa przedmieścia, które do XVIII w. dominowały w układzie przestrzennym Nowego Sącza: na południu Węgierskie (inaczej Większe lub Wielkie) regularnie zabudowane, zaś na wschód od miasta, na prawym brzegu rzeki Kamienicy Zakamienica (Mniejsze). „I” Obejmuje północną część Nowego Sącza między Dunajcem a Kamienicą do Plant. Zaznaczono granice miasta, zabudowania, zieleń i działki. Widoczne są dwa mosty – na Kamienicy i Dunajcu. W miejscu obecnej ulicy Jagiellońskiej, wychodzącej z Rynku, znajduje się ulica Węgierska „Ungarische Gasse”. Obok granicy miasta napisy „CHEłMIEC” i „ZAłUBINCZE” – wsie sąsiadujące z Nowym Sączem.

„II” Obejmuje wschodnią część Nowego Sącza z dzielnicą „Za Kamienica” sąsiadującą z przylegającymi do granic miasta wsiami: „ZAłUBIńCZE”, „NASCISZOWA”, „GOLĄBKOWICE”. Na mapie zaznaczono drogę do Grybowa „nach Grybow”, potok łubinka „Lubinka Bach”, pola, zieleń i kilka zabudowań. „III” Obejmuje fragment zachodniej części miasta przylegającej do wsi „SWINIARSKO”. Granica zachodnia miasta biegnie wzdłuż jednej z odnóg Dunajca. Przy linii granicznej napis: „Praetensionslinie der Gemeinde Neu Sandec”. Od granicy miasta odbiega linia oznaczająca „Pretensions Linie der Gemeinde Swinarskie”. Na mapie zaznaczono rzeki: Dunajec „Dunajec Fluss” i Poprad „Poprad Fluss”, potok Dąbrówka „Dabrowka Bach”, tereny z zielenią. „IV” Obejmuje „Węgierskie przedmieście”, „Podgórze”, „łany”, „Mlyny Hamry i Poddębie”. Zaznaczono: „St Nicolaus”, oznaczający kościół św. Mikołaja – obecnie nieistniejący. Na mapie zaznaczono ulice, zabudowania, tereny zielone, rzeki: Dunajec „Dunajec Fluss”, Poprad „Poprad Fluss”, Kamienicę „Kamienica Bach” i potoki: Młynówkę „Mühlbach” i łącznik „łaźnik Bach”. „V” Obejmuje wschodnią część miasta: „Paswisko wielkie” „Braeuhaus”, „Mlyny Hamry i Poddębie”, sąsiadujące ze wsiami „GOłĄBKOWICE” i „FALKOWA”. Zaznaczono rzekę Kamienicę „Kamienica Bach” i jej dopływy – potoki: Młynówka „Mühlbach” i łącznik „łaźnik Bach”, zabudowania oraz tereny z zielenią. „VI” Obejmuje południowo-zachodnią część Nowego Sącza – dzielnicę „Podgórze” sąsiadującą ze wsią „SWINIARSKO” i „DĄBRÓWKA”. Zaznaczono fragmenty rzek: Dunajca „Dunajec Fluss” i Popradu „Poprad Fluss”, potoku Dąbrówka „Dąbrwka Bach” oraz zabudowania i obszary z zielenią. „VII” Obejmuje fragment południowej części – dzielnicy „łany” i „Podgorze” przylegające do sąsiedniej wsi „DĄBRÓWKA”. Zaznaczono drogę do Starego Sącza „von Alt Sandec”, obszary z zielenią, zabudowania, pola, bardzo mały fragment potoku Dąbrówka „Dąbrwka Bach” oraz linie: „Praetensionslinie der Gem. Swiniarsko” i „Paetensionslinie der Gemeinde Neu Sandec”. „VIII” Obejmuje fragment południowej części miasta – dzielnicę „Gorzkow” i „łany” przylegające od południa do wsi „ZAWADA” i od wschodu do wsi „FALKOWA”. Zaznaczono „Paswisko wielkie”, a przy granicy miasta z Falkową linię „Praetensionslinie der Gemeinde Falkowa”, rzekę Kamienicę „Kamienica Bach”, potok łącznik „łaźnik Bach”, drogi w kierunku Zawady „nach Zawada” i Muszyny ”nach Muszina”, zabudowania, obszary z zielenią, pola. „ad. VIII” Obejmuje fragment wschodniej części miasta z dzielnicą „Gorzkow” przylegającą od południa do wsi „ZAWADA” i od wschodu do wsi „JAMNICA” i „FALKOWA”. Zaznaczono fragment rzeki Kamienica „Kamienicae Bach” płynącej równolegle do granicy miasta. „IX” Obejmuje fragment południowej części miasta – „łany” przylegające do wsi „DĄBRÓWKA” i „ZAWADA”.
